Senses.Explanation: To roam freely according to one's nature is a recurrent description of unconstrained conduct, usually paired with being open according to conditions. Nanyue Huairang gives the pair when asked how to preserve the matter without later trouble, while later hall speakers apply it to movement through every direction. Yongjue Yuanxian also blocks a shallow reading: merely being directionless and loose is still far from home. The corpus therefore uses the expression both affirmatively and as a phrase whose imitation can be rejected.

Senses.Explanation: To take its own course or proceed without forced direction. The compound is attested. Yuanwu Keqin gives an explicit comparison: 'what is called proceeding of itself is like a dull-witted person whose household has a capable person caring for him.' Other records pair it with following circumstances in both word orders, with freedom, and with the doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself.' Concrete lines place it after drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry, or say that at all times and places one proceeds of oneself freely and responds without a fixed direction. Zen bends an everyday expression for running its own course into descriptions of conduct and response, but the evidence does not turn it into passivity or one uniform instruction.

Senses.Note: Two independently allowlisted J23 records preserve the exact seventh-section heading. Their wording is closely related, but each anchors the title as a title.

Senses.Explanation: Freely following the course is a fixed evaluative formula for unhindered comportment. Masters reverse and repeat its halves, pair it with being free and unencumbered, and set it after the thorough integration of teaching and worldly affairs. Feiyin Tongrong playfully reverses “buoyant and unforced” and “unforced and buoyant” before trampling the old holy monk. Gaofeng Yuanmiao pairs the formula with being unconstrained east, west, north, and south. Gaofeng's Essentials joins it to being free, unencumbered, dry, and clean after penetrating both teaching and worldly distinctions. The formula therefore evaluates comportment publicly; it is not merely an adverb meaning ‘automatically.’

Senses.Explanation: Moving a step is ordinary bodily movement made diagnostic in Chan positional language. Masters demand it after sustained exertion, pair it with turning the body, or place it before a bright hall: the step tests whether a respondent can leave the position already occupied. Hansong Zhicao says that strenuous pressure still is not ‘moving a step’; when he asks whether the assembly knows the move, he shouts ‘put it down.’ Zhe'an Jingfan pairs moving a step with turning the body in the work of an effective teacher. Hongzhi Zhengjue places moving a step before the bright-moon hall beside turning the mechanism on a crystal ground. The repeated positional pair shows a demanded shift, while ordinary travel occurrences remain a falsification class.

“Turns instead into poison” marks a reversal in which something excellent becomes harmful because its recipient cannot use it. Yuanwu Keqin contrasts Nanquan’s words as the finest clarified butter for a living-eyed listener with poison for a dead one. Tianyin Yuanxiu applies the same reversal to people who force Linji’s devices into fixed theory. Poshan Haiming uses it for someone half hungry and half full who will not approach the food, and Guxue Zhenzhe for students who resent a teacher’s sharp correction.
Senses.Note: The usual subject is fine teaching or nourishment. The reversal concerns its effect on the recipient, not literal poisoning.

Senses.Explanation: 翻轉面皮 means “change one's face”: make a deliberate about-face or set one’s visible bearing differently. Yunju uses the image critically, whereas Dahui makes it a requirement; Juelang turns their inherited dispute into a lightning-fast reversal. Poshan and Lingji actively commend a changed face, but Zhe’an frames the stubborn speaker’s account as a boast and then rebukes its one-sidedness.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 如絃行人若問窮通事鐵壁銀山在面前丹霞燒木佛火燒木佛丹霞罪脫落鬚眉院主災一陣東風回暖律幾多春色上梅腮則監寺叅青峯法眼丙丁童子公案觸著神鋒劈面揮電光石火較猶遅不因洗耳池邊過肯信人間有是非丹霞訪龐居士靈照提籃因緣放籃斂手舉籃歸自是多情惹是非月落畫堂人去後不堪歡笑只堪悲兜率和尚三關性在甚處赤脚波斯叩海門黑風吹浪暗昏昏三更掣斷青霞鎻笑看驪龍戲子孫四大分散作

Senses.Explanation: “Lightning flash and stone spark” names an extremely rapid moment. The retained witnesses explicitly call it still too slow, make recognition at that speed decisive, and say pursuit cannot catch it.
